Its author's self-designation as the elder links it closely to 3 John, which shares the same title and the same concern with the reception of traveling teachers.

The letter is distinctive for turning the community's theological conflict into a practical rule about hospitality, addressing whom to welcome rather than expounding doctrine at length. Its figurative address to the elect lady and her children - most likely a personified congregation rather than an individual - is a further distinctive touch, and its brevity means it has left scholars with little basis for firm conclusions about its author or precise setting.

3John.name: 3 John
3John.blurb:
Third John is a short personal letter, among the briefest books in the Bible, written by the elder to an individual named Gaius and concerned with a concrete dispute over hospitality within a local community. It commends Gaius for welcoming and supporting traveling teachers who had gone out for the sake of the name, sharply criticizes a man named Diotrephes who refused such hospitality and even expelled those who offered it, and commends a third figure, Demetrius. It offers a rare, unusually specific glimpse into the tensions and personalities of an early congregation.

The letter is structured around three named individuals. It opens with a warm greeting and prayer for Gaius and praise for his faithfulness in supporting traveling workers (verses 1-8); it then turns to Diotrephes, who loves to be first, rejects the elder's authority, and refuses to receive the brothers (9-10); and it closes by commending Demetrius, who is well spoken of by all, before expressing the hope of a personal visit and sending final greetings (11-15).
3John.attribution: Like 2 John, this letter is written by one who calls himself the elder and is traditionally linked with John and the Johannine circle. Scholars associate the three Johannine letters with the same community and setting, dating them to the late first century, while leaving the elder's identity open. Its short length limits firm conclusions.
3John.setting: The letter is addressed to an individual named Gaius and concerns the reception of traveling teachers within the community. It refers to a figure named Diotrephes who had refused such hospitality. The setting is a concrete dispute over authority and welcome in a local community.
3John.themes:
Hospitality toward traveling workers is the letter's central concern, praised in Gaius, who has supported the brothers who went out depending on the welcome of local communities (verses 5-8), and treated as a way of sharing in the work of the truth. Support for such itinerant teachers emerges as a practical expression of fellowship in a movement that relied on networks of hospitality.

Conflict over authority supplies the letter's sharper theme, focused in the figure of Diotrephes, who refuses to acknowledge the elder, spreads malicious talk, declines to receive the traveling brothers, and even expels those who would (verses 9-10). Set against him is the commended Demetrius, and the contrast between welcome and refusal, humility and self-assertion, gives this short note its drama - a rare window onto a personal power struggle within an early community.
3John.distinctives:
Third John is the shortest book in the New Testament by word count and belongs with 1 and 2 John to the Johannine letters, sharing the self-designation of the elder with 2 John and, with it, a concern for the reception of traveling teachers; the two brief letters are natural companions, treating the same practical issue from different sides - one warning against welcoming false teachers, the other rebuking a failure to welcome legitimate ones.

The letter is distinctive for being addressed to a named individual about a specific local situation, and for the vividness with which it names and characterizes the parties to a congregational quarrel, especially the domineering Diotrephes. This concreteness gives it unusual value as evidence for the frictions over authority and hospitality in an early community, even as its brevity leaves the underlying dispute and the identities involved largely unexplained.

Jude.name: Jude
Jude.blurb:
Jude is a brief, forceful letter occupying a single chapter, written to urge its readers to contend for the faith against teachers who had infiltrated the community and whose conduct and doctrine the author condemns in vehement terms. Setting aside a more general letter he had intended to write, Jude turns instead to warning, denouncing the intruders as ungodly people who pervert grace into license, and marshaling a striking series of examples of past judgment - drawn from both the Old Testament and Jewish tradition outside it - to assure his readers of the fate awaiting such people. He closes by exhorting the faithful to build themselves up and to keep themselves in the love of God.

The short letter moves from occasion to denunciation to exhortation. It opens by explaining the shift to an urgent appeal to contend for the faith once delivered (verses 1-4); it then denounces the false teachers at length, illustrating their certain judgment through a cascade of examples and vivid images and citing prophecies against them (5-16); and it closes by calling the faithful to persevere, to keep themselves in God's love, and to have mercy on the wavering, ending with a memorable doxology (17-25).
Jude.attribution: The letter names Jude, described as a brother of James, traditionally understood as a brother of Jesus. Scholars are divided over whether it stems from that figure or was written later in his name, and its date is uncertain. Its literary relationship to 2 Peter, which shares much of its content, figures in the discussion.
Jude.setting: The letter addresses communities troubled by teachers whose conduct and teaching the author condemns. Its audience is urged to hold to received belief against these figures. The setting is one of perceived internal threat, described in vivid and allusive terms.
Jude.themes:
Contending for the inherited faith is the letter's explicit purpose, stated at the outset as an urgent appeal to defend the faith once for all delivered against those who had crept in unnoticed (verses 3-4). The integrity of the received teaching, and the danger posed by those who distort grace into a pretext for immorality, frame the whole.

The certainty of judgment on the false teachers is the letter's dominant theme, driven home by an accumulation of examples of past judgment and by vivid images of the intruders as blemishes, waterless clouds, and wandering stars (verses 5-16). Against this denunciation stands the closing call to the faithful to persevere - to build themselves up, keep themselves in the love of God, and show mercy to those who doubt (17-23) - so that condemnation of error serves a pastoral end, and the letter ends not on judgment but on a doxology of confidence in God's keeping power.
Jude.distinctives:
Jude is one of the shortest books in the New Testament and belongs to the General Epistles, and its most discussed feature is its close relationship to 2 Peter, the central section of which overlaps so extensively with Jude that most scholars conclude one drew on the other, with the majority regarding Jude as the earlier and 2 Peter as dependent on it. This makes the pair a key case study in literary relationships within the New Testament.

The letter is further distinguished by its citation of writings outside the Old Testament canon - it alludes to a dispute over the body of Moses and quotes a prophecy attributed to Enoch - which raises questions about the scope of scripture the author regarded as authoritative and has drawn attention throughout the history of interpretation. Its vehement, image-laden denunciation and its polished doxology give the tiny letter a distinctive intensity.
outline: Greeting and the call to contend for the faith (1–4)
Examples and denunciation of the ungodly (5–16)
Exhortation to the faithful and closing doxology (17–25)

Rev.name: Revelation
Rev.blurb:
Revelation is the final book of the New Testament and its one full-scale apocalypse, a work of visionary prophecy written to seven churches in the Roman province of Asia and unfolding through a dazzling sequence of symbolic visions. Presenting itself as the revelation given to a prophet named John while in exile, it opens with messages to the seven churches addressing their particular strengths and failures, then sweeps into a series of heavenly visions - a throne, a scroll sealed with seven seals, trumpets, cosmic conflict, beasts, and bowls of wrath - that dramatize the struggle between God and the powers arrayed against him, and drive toward the overthrow of evil, the last judgment, and the appearance of a new heaven and earth.

The book proceeds through interlocking cycles of sevens. After the opening vision of the exalted Christ and the letters to the seven churches (chapters 1-3), it moves to the throne room, the scroll, and the seven seals (4-7), the seven trumpets (8-11), and then a central section on the conflict with the dragon and the beasts and the seven bowls of wrath (12-18), before culminating in the final defeat of evil, the last judgment, and the vision of the new Jerusalem descending, where God dwells with humanity and all things are made new (19-22).
Rev.attribution: The book names its author as John, and tradition often identified him with the apostle, though the writer describes himself simply as a servant and prophet. Scholars debate whether this John is the apostle, another figure of the same name, or a distinct prophet, and generally date the work to the late first century, commonly the reign of Domitian around 95 CE. An earlier date is also argued by some.
Rev.setting: The book addresses seven specific churches in the Roman province of Asia, amid pressures the author frames as conflict with imperial power and surrounding society. Its audience faces hostility and the temptation to accommodate. The Roman imperial context pervades its imagery.
Rev.themes:
The sovereignty of God over history and its powers is Revelation's central affirmation, staged in the throne-room vision where all creation worships the one seated on the throne and the slain but victorious Lamb (chapters 4-5), an image that governs the whole and reframes the conflicts that follow as subordinate to God's rule. Judgment on evil and on the oppressive powers - depicted through the beasts and the great city under imperial imagery - runs through the cycles of seals, trumpets, and bowls toward the final overthrow (6-18).

Faithful endurance is the answering pastoral theme: the letters to the churches (2-3) call for perseverance, repentance, and resistance to compromise, and the visions are designed to strengthen a pressured community by disclosing the true, unseen outcome of its struggle. The book culminates in the promise of a renewed creation, the new Jerusalem where God dwells with his people and death and mourning are no more (21-22), so that its message to the seven churches is finally one of hope grounded in the certainty of God's triumph.
Rev.distinctives:
Revelation is the New Testament's sole example of a full apocalypse, a genre marked by symbolic visions mediated by heavenly figures, and this sets it apart from every other book in the collection; its nearest canonical relatives are the visionary sections of Daniel and Ezekiel, on whose imagery it draws so heavily that it can seem woven from the Old Testament prophets, though it never quotes them directly. It also presents itself as a letter and as prophecy, combining three forms in one work.

The book is distinctive for the density and difficulty of its symbolism - its beasts, numbers, and cosmic imagery - and for the long, contested history of its interpretation, which has yielded readings that treat it as a coded commentary on its own Roman setting, as a forecast of history, as a symbolic drama of enduring conflict, or as a vision of the end. Its concentration of Old Testament allusion, especially from the prophets, and its role as the canon's concluding vision of judgment and new creation give it a singular place among the Scriptures.
outline: Vision of the Son of Man and letters to the seven churches (1–3)
The throne, the scroll, and the seven seals (4–7)
Conflict, the beasts, and the bowls of wrath (12–18)
Final judgment and the new creation (19–22)
